If this condition is met at time t, we can observe the angle at which point p makes with the normal to the edge of the polygon as the angle at which the robot located at that edge looks towards point p. The model we used is a two-dimensional array of photonic crystal waveplates. Each waveplate is made up of a light beam splitter and a birefringent crystal. The purpose of the beam splitter is to split a polarized electromagnetic wave into its component polarizations. The crystal then affects the wave's phase velocity based on the polarization. The model exhibits two distinct frequencies of operation - one for coupling and one for braking. The coupling frequency corresponds to a point where the model's dispersion diagram intersects at a single point, indicating a high degree of coupling among the waves. The braking frequency, on the other hand, corresponds to a point where the model's dispersion diagram intersects at three distinct points, indicating a high degree of wave braking and photon trapping. The model's ability to display both coupling and braking frequencies within a narrow frequency band makes it an ideal candidate for enhancing sensitivity in optical devices such as filters and resonators. The term "magnetic mirror" has been commonly used to describe this type of metamaterial, although it is more accurately referred to as a "photonic crystal waveplate mirror". The term "magnetic mirror" is misleading as it implies a effect caused by magnetism as opposed to birefringence. The term "waveplate mirror" better conveys the role of the waveplate in the model's functionality. The term "waveplate mirror" can be further divided into two subcategories - "X-type" and "Lambda-type" waveplate mirrors. The "X-type" waveplate mirror displays an "X" shaped dispersion diagram while the "Lambda-type" waveplate mirror displays a "Lambda" shaped dispersion diagram. Both the "X-type" and "Lambda-type" waveplate mirrors can serve as frequency brakes in a range that spans from the coupling frequency to the braking frequency. The term "X-type" and "Lambda-type" waveplate mirrors refers to the shape of their dispersion diagrams as opposed to the shape of the waveplate itself. The shape of the waveplate is actually a rectangle. The term "X-type" and "Lambda-type" waveplate mirrors can also be determined by the orientation of the light waves as they propagate through the model. The "X-type" waveplate mirror is characterized by light waves that propagate at an angle of 120 degrees while the "Lambda-type" waveplate mirror is characterized by light waves that propagate at an angle of 60 degrees. To compute the relative entropy, we utilize Monte Carlo simulations. The results reveal that the distribution of redshifts exhibits a skewed, non-uniform pattern. The Monte Carlo methods we employed to compute these values also enabled us to generate typical sets of redshifts. These sets can serve as input for simulations that model the formation of galaxies and can be compared to observed data via the Monte Carlo method we developed. This method involves applying the cumulative distribution function to obtain the expected values of the observed quantities and assessing their agreement with the actual observed values via the relative entropy. The same method yields a relative entropy of 0.69 when applied to the Tully-Fisher law. Initially, the method was tested on a stationary airfoil in a turbulent, incompressible fluid with a singular boundary layer, then on a moving airfoil in a turbulent, incompressible fluid without a singular boundary layer for both high and low Reynolds numbers. To validate the results, we compared them to experimental data and other numerical methods. Our analysis focused on determining if the method accurately handles the effects of a moving surface on boundary layer turbulence. Our findings show that the spectral reconstruction method in the complex frequency plane effectively simulates the dynamics of a moving airfoil in a turbulent, incompressible fluid with discontinuous boundary layers, accurately capturing the features seen in experiments and other numerical methods. Our approach also successfully demonstrated its ability to handle the effects of a moving surface on boundary layer turbulence. Our next step will be to apply this method to simulate the flow around moving surfaces with complex geometries at various Reynolds numbers. Due to its limited scope, the current study did not include visualizations of the streamlines and the distribution of the pressure coefficient. We intend to address this limitation in the future.   shock model that includes their interaction with the dust-driven snowline,

  simulation. Our analysis also involved studying the asymmetry of lines in 
  the spectra of these stars, a phenomenon we found to be closely

  specifically its relation to bulk geometry and the variation of
  entanglement entropy across all dimensions. By applying this approach,
  we derive precise insights into the quantum length's behavior in both
  two-dimensional conformal field theories and three-dimensional topological
  insulators. Our findings also extend to higher-dimensional scenarios.
  Notably, we find that the quantum length represents a form of effective
  cross ratio that can be determined from the zero-point fluctuations
  present in the holographic bulk. In essence, we re-express the
  holographic quantum York-Shenker length as a weighted sum of
  geodesic distances set within the bulk. This new formulation
  offers a more fundamental understanding of the zero-point fluctuations
  and their direct link to the quantum length. In addition, we
  investigate the variation of entanglement entropy across all
  dimensions and define the quantum length's gradient for each
  dimensional scenario. Our research is supported by a variety of
  holographic models, including those that simulate the properties
  of two-dimensional CFTs and three-dimensional topological insulators.  We
  also introduce the concept of a bulk operator's squared mass as a
  key factor that dictates the geometry of zero-point fluctuations. 
  Consequently, we find that the quantum length's gradient across all
  dimensions is entirely determined by this squared mass. As such,
  we establish a direct link between the quantum length's gradient
  and the holographic bulk's geometry, which in turn is influenced
  by the physical properties of the corresponding CFT or topological
  insulator. Moreover, we find that the geodesic distance, when
  squared, represents a form of effective cross ratio that can be
  determined from the zero-point fluctuations present in the holographic
  bulk. This new insight offers a precise, holographic understanding
  of the quantum York-Shenker length and its related properties. 
  As such, we believe that our research provides a solid foundation
  for further, in-depth analyses of zero-point fluctuations. 
  Consequently, we anticipate that our findings will be highly
  valuable in the study of holographic theories. 
  Furthermore, we believe that our results will be useful in 
  the analysis of zero-point fluctuations within string theory. 
  As such, we have made our research openly available in the 
  hope that it will be built upon

  a computational approach to creating humor by combining three elements:
  a setup, a twist, and a punchline. Initially, it generates a twist from

  possible punchlines are produced by manipulating the twist. If the result
  is not a well-defined joke, the model refines the twist until it does.

  it enables the automatic creation of original jokes, it generalizes well
  to new setups, and it can produce multiple variants of a joke. In tests,
  humans found the generated jokes to be a significant portion (75%) funny,
  and they preferred (60%) jokes produced by this method over those created
  through association. This approach has implications for developing more
  sophisticated AI humor capabilities. This research is applied to a simple
  text-based game where the goal is to make the character laugh by inputting
  jokes. In the evaluation, the character's laughter increased (45%) when jokes
  were generated using this method versus relying on association.  Well-defined
  jokes can be evaluated using a metric called joke complexity, which is
  calculated by counting the number of words until the punchline is reached.
  However, this metric has a limitation called the word hurdle, which is
  the minimum number of words required to convey a twist. As a result, this
  metric cannot distinguish between jokes with similar complexity. To address
  this issue, a new metric called the twist distance is proposed, which is
  calculated by identifying the words that characterize the twist and then
  determining the distance between them. This distance is found to be a more
  reliable indicator of the humor mechanism in a joke. The evaluation of
  this metric shows that it can predict funny jokes with a high degree of
  accuracy (80%). This research is applicable to a broader context, as it

Plasmids are small circles of DNA that can be shared among bacteria, allowing the transfer of antibiotic resistance traits. We've developed an mathematical immunology approach that considers the dynamics of plasmid carriage, infection rates, and antibiotic use. Although previous models assumed a perfect plasmid transmission system, our model allows for an imperfect transfer of plasmids. We found that both the initial spread and coexistence phases of plasmid-mediated resistance are influenced by the accuracy of plasmid transfer. In fact, we discovered that there are plasmid transfer thresholds that either promote the spread of resistance or lead to its decline. Our research also reveals that bacteria carrying plasmids can coexist with antibiotic use in some cases. However, we found that even if resistance does not dominate in these situations, it can still persist and eventually become dominant over time. This is known as the "rebound effect." We were able to derive conditions under which this rebound effect occurs and it is influenced by the accuracy of plasmid transfer. Our model predicts that the spread of plasmid-mediated resistance can take on a bistable pattern, whereas the geometry of these stability domains is determined by the plasmid transfer threshold and the effect of plasmid carriage on infection and death rates. We tested this hypothesis through simulations conducted using a more detailed model. Our results also highlight the importance of considering the dynamics of plasmid carriage in the model. We believe that our model provides valuable insights into the spread of plasmid-mediated resistance and can serve as a foundation for further research into this topic.   matter. Here, we go a step further by determining the form of the density

  compatibility of this method with existing data on the density dependence in a

  nucleon-nucleon interaction and the density of states in nuclear matter.

  suitable for describing the behavior of the density dependence at finite densities.

  information with that from other sources, such as cosmic ray and big bang nucleosynthesis
  data, and for using it in nuclear density functionals for extended Thomas-Fermi

This method involves extracting the vacuum polarization function from data on atomic energy levels or from direct experiments, and then using that information to calculate the contribution to the anomalous magnetic moment.  This approach can provide a more precise determination of the anomalous magnetic moment, surpassing the current limits set by experiments, and is especially crucial for the muon's anomalous magnetic moment as it is primarily affected by hadronic interactions.  To apply this method, we need to re-analyse existing data on atomic energy levels and direct experiments for the vacuum polarization, and use statistical tools to evaluate the resulting precisions.  We also propose possible experiments that could further refine our understanding of the hadronic contribution to the anomalous magnetic moment.  In conclusion, we can currently estimate the hadronic contribution to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment with a precision of 0.93 parts per thousand, and predict that the planned Muon g-2 experiment will be able to reduce this limit to 0.23 parts per thousand.  For the electron, we can estimate its hadronic contribution with a precision of 1.04 parts per million, and predict that the planned Electron Muon Scattering Experiment at the Fermilab will be able to reduce this limit to 0.052 parts per million.  Overall, we believe that with the planned experiments and a re-analysis of existing data, the hadronic contribution to the anomalous magnetic moment will be determined with a precision that is several orders of magnitude better than currently achieved through hadronic models.  As such, the limiting precision of the anomalous magnetic moment will then be set by the experimental limitations, rather than the hadronic contribution.  We also emphasize the importance of complementary experiments that can provide a more precise understanding of the hadronic contribution to the anomalous magnetic moment, and highlight the potential of existing and future facilities in this regard.   from collisions involving certain subatomic particles called long-lived
  particles. As these particles decay slowly, they can travel considerable
  distances before breaking down, leading to rare and difficult-to-detect end
  products. In the search for these elusive particles, I present two novel
  approaches to effectively scan for their signatures within existing data from
  the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The first method targets particles with
  very short decay radii by utilizing the ATLAS detector's magnetic field
  to steer charged decay products towards the detector's center, thus
  enhancing detection chances. The second approach focuses on particles with
  longer decay lengths by employing a new strategy to identify events with
  significant missing transverse momentum in the momentum range between 400
  GeV and 5 TeV, which to date remains largely unexplored. By implementing
  these optimized search strategies on the complete LHC dataset collected at
  13 TeV, I demonstrate the potential to significantly improve detection limits
  for a wide range of long-lived particles beyond their current constraints. 
  In the process, I highlight the analytical and simulated evidence for
  previously unreported constraints on particles like the axion-like monopole
  and the scalar inflaton, as well as the tangible guidance for further
  experimental developments to combat the limitations posed by these
  notoriously difficult-to-detect particles. 
  The proposed search strategies are made publicly available through an
  interactive tool called LHaS, which allows for tailored implementations
  based on various experimental conditions and detector configurations. 
  This research also paves the way for potential analyses on the underlying
  physics models at the theoretical level, as well as concrete suggestions
  for future collider experiments with upgraded detectors capable of handling
  higher energy collisions. 
  In the analysis, I utilize the ATLAS detector simulation at the LHC, but
  similar searches can be implemented on other particle colliders using
  different experimental setups.

  includes solutions for potential issues such as beam scattering, fake
  leptons, and photon misidentification. 
  The code also includes optimized reconstruction configurations for
  long-lived particles that could serve as benchmarks for future
  experiments.

  mechanism that bridges the gap between different action/observation pairs, resulting in a model that is both

concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) has developed from a simple extension of the syndrome decoding approach to encompass a wide range of applications in coding theory, including code construction and an analysis of existing codes. Specifically, in the realm of algebraic codes, Raptor codes and Virtuous codes can be viewed as variants of OGS, demonstrating the versatility and breadth of coding theory. This article presents an in-depth examination of the ordered generating sequence framework, along with a detailed exploration of its underlying mathematics. We also delve into the theoretical foundations of Raptor codes and Virtuous codes, in addition to an exploration of recent research that has delved into the study of codes through the lens of OGS, with a focus on linear codes and their successive cancellation decoding process. This exploration has resulted in a range of novel code constructions, including irreducible polynomials, the Kautz construction, and Thue-Morse codes, among others. Through this in-depth examination, we aim to provide a comprehensive and unified understanding of the principles and methods employed in the design of good codes using the ordered generating sequence framework. This understanding is accompanied by an analysis of the future directions of this line of research. This article is an expanded version of the authors' previous presentation on the same topic presented at ISIT 2022. In this model, all motion is linear, dependent on previous positions, and results in a linear expansion of the system's configuration. We have shown that this model accurately mimics the behavior of a classical harmonic oscillator and mass-spring system, both at rest and in motion. where two separate atomic membranes, separated by a distance, interact through a shared classical electromagnetic field. As a result of this interaction, the atomic membranes become entangled, exhibiting "quantum nonlocality." If one of the atomic membranes is illuminated with a monochromatic light, the resulting pattern of interference contains a distinctive "antibunching" pattern, a hallmark of quantum behavior. Following this initial illumination, a shift in the spatial distribution of coherence from a Gaussian distribution to a sinusoidal distribution occurs over time. This change in distribution is attributed to the nonlocal effects of quantum entanglement rather than any direct interaction with the light. As a result, this system can serve as an example for demonstrating the presence of quantum nonlocality without the need for interference experiments. Moreover, this investigation also explores the spread of coherence in both free space and through optical fiber, revealing that this system may be utilized for directing quantum nonlocality in a controlled manner. Finally, this research indicates that even minimal systems, like the one studied here, are capable of exhibiting complex quantum behavior that can only be fully understood by considering the system's full wavefunction. We have made our numerical code available online to facilitate further investigation of this system. We have also proposed an experimental setup for realizing this system, and have identified that the key challenge in implementing this system is minimizing loss in the setup while maintaining the integrity of the quantum nonlocality. We have further demonstrated that any loss can be accounted for by replacing the atomic membranes with their corresponding decay rates, and that this description is applicable even when the decay rates are themselves entangled. We have also developed an approach for generating a controlled amount of pair photons from this system by shining a strong classical light on one of the membranes, and have estimated that it is feasible to achieve a pair production rate of approximately 10^4 pairs per second from a system of 10 membranes. We have also proposed an approach for detecting these pair photons by utilizing a highly efficient photon detector, and have estimated that it is feasible to detect all the information associated with a single pair photon, including its spatial distribution, momentum, and polarization, by utilizing a combination of highly efficient detectors and a sophisticated analysis technique. We have further demonstrated that it is feasible to extend this system to utilize multiple atomic membranes arranged in various configurations, and that this extension can serve as an example for demonstrating the presence of quantum nonlocality without the need for interference experiments.   \textit{adaptive Chunks Through Hole} (ATCH) with significant improvements

  success of Chunks Through Hole (CTH), ATCH enhances the approach by
  incorporating the inherent structural regularities in archive files and

  ATCH outperforms other compression methods like LZ77, DEFLATE, and

  ratios than Snappy at lower speeds and better speeds than Zstandard at
  similar compression ratios. This indicates that ATCH can either significantly
  reduce data sizes at manageable computational costs or compute the
  representations of data sets at rapid speeds at comparable data sizes.

  It discusses the advantages of using a regular grammar in place of prefix
  codes to represent compressed data, resulting in ATCH's notable speed
  improvements while maintaining comparable compression ratios. It also
  explores the ATCH's potential applications in binary protocol format
  compression and its relevant code is available for public use.  It can be
  used as a replacement for Snappy in scenarios where faster compression

  compact, weighing around 20KB, and is thus suitable for embedding in

  speeds and return the compressed representations of larger data sets at
  manageable computational costs. It can also be used to compress larger

  Sommerfeld obstacle exclusion principle, which describes how signal delay

  in realistic scenarios with multiple signal paths and varying signal strengths.

  on low-power devices. Our results indicate that accounting for signal delay
  reduces position calculation error and yields more accurate position estimates.

  error is more than twice as large as signal delay, which means that delaying
  signals by 100 meters results in a position calculation error of at least 50 meters.

  measurements or simulated using models like our frequency domain analysis.

  of about 5 meters and signal delay with an accuracy of around 20 meters.

  classification rely heavily on selecting informative queries and
  aggregating pool data. These methods often overlook the significant
  benefits of actively obtaining additional relevant data through
  rejections. Existing rejection-based AL techniques neglect valuable
  information encoded in classification uncertainties, mechanically applying
  fixed sampling probabilities to all data points without consideration
  of their individual importance. We propose a novel Active Learning
  framework, RejectionAwareAL (RAAL), addressing these shortcomings.
  RAAL assigns query labels to the most uncertain and valuable data
  points prioritizing new acquisitions and cost-effective pool data
  utilization. Our method's performance is evaluated across seven real-
  world datasets, demonstrating RAAL outperforms traditional AL methods
  by a 20\% reduction in target sizes while achieving comparable or
  superior performance results. Notably, RAAL exhibits notable improvements
  when applied to datasets with varying noise levels, demonstrating its
  robustness in handling label errors. Our approach provide valuable
  insights into optimizing target sizes and pool data utilization in AL
  scenarios. We make RAAL's code and models publicly available at
  \url{https://github.com/AIForAllIA/RejectionAwareActiveLearning}. 
  We hope RAAL's contributions spark further research and practical
  applications in efficient, data-efficient machine learning. 
  We also establish RAAL's feasibility in real-world deployments, as
  evidenced by our successful implementation of a conversational AI
  system that employs RAAL to continuously learn from user interactions. 
  This experience-led knowledge updates result in a 30% reduction in
  new interactions being generated to achieve the same performance
  results compared to using a static model.  We believe RAAL's
  advantages will be particularly beneficial in large-scale, long-
  term, costly supervised training dependencies.

  strategies to handle already labeled data points that were

A new concept for a gravitational wave detector based on a Kerr parameter of $10^{55}$ aims to surpass this limit by utilizing a high-power laser to generate a bright quantum field, thereby counteracting photon noise through back-action.  A key aspect of achieving this progress is the development of a stable, coherent light source with a high photon number and low phase-space variance when switching between detection and illumination modes.  To assess the performance of this detector, we must evaluate the impact of its own light on its own quantum noise, effectively needing to solve the Heisenberg equation for a coherent state's Wigner function.  In the course of exploring this equation's solution, we derive the Wigner function of the coherent state itself, yielding a new expression for the phase-space variance that differs from conventional estimates by incorporating the influence of back-action noise and light scattering.  As a result, we find that the sensitivity of this detector concept is superior to the standard quantum limit by a factor equal to its Kerr parameter.  Consequently, all Kerr-based gravitational wave detectors will exceed the standard quantum limit, providing a key insight for optimizing these devices.  Ultimately, our research implies that the effectiveness of these detectors will be constrained by their ability to maintain a bright, stable light source rather than reliance on advanced technologies like squeezing or optomechanical enhancement.  The implications of this finding extend beyond Kerr-based detectors to any light-based experiment seeking to surpass the standard quantum limit. However, EEG's limited spatial resolution poses a significant challenge for its application in source localisation problems. The lack of clear solutions hinders its potential for certain tasks such as brain computer interface development and neurological disorder diagnosis. The limited spatial resolution of EEG can be viewed as a compressed version of brain signal, offering a compressed sensing application. The sparse reconstruction method, based on dictionary learning, has shown considerable performance in processing other compressed signals. Consequently, we investigated two sparse representation methods, N-way Non-negative Sparse Coding (NNSC) and Multi-way Sparse Coding (MWSC), on three datasets. The results revealed that NNSC and MWSC achieved high signal-to-noise ratio values of 8.35 and 8.51, respectively, compared to 7.58 obtained using a general sparse representation method. The evaluation of these methods on real EEG data indicated that NNSC and MWSC yielded root mean square errors of 3.4 and 3.5, respectively, below the threshold of 0.05, demonstrating their effectiveness in reconstructing brain activity via EEG. The analysis of performance limitations revealed that better results could be achieved by enhancing the dictionary learning process. The research was validated by an independent group that utilized MWSC for source localisation in EEG and obtained an accuracy of 0.83. The evaluation of MWSC on a realistic head model showed that it could effectively handle various scalp EEG lead fields, cementing its position as an excellent option for brain computer interface development and neurological disorder diagnosis. We propose a novel two-step approach for inter-domain image translation.
First, we perform single-domain image translation on the source dataset.
Then, we employ a reverse translation to obtain the corresponding image
in the target dataset.
We achieve notable results on five distinct datasets: Caltech-256, FLIC, PFBD, CIP, and VOC.
In particular, we successfully cross-translate images between three datasets without any prior knowledge of the target domain.
Our model exhibits robust performance, surpassing non-adversarial baselines in 0.31% to 6.08% mAP scores.
We demonstrate that our model can be utilized as a regularizer to enhance the robustness of a single-domain target model.
Our method yields superior results compared to existing interpolation techniques, with an mAP score increase of up to 5.03%.
We make our code publicly available at https://github.com/zheng752/ImageNet-Translatior.  \newpage{}

  In the context of linear systems with multiple inputs and multiple outputs, 
  where high-dimensional matrices are composed from lower-rank building blocks, 
  decay in lambda values (eigenvalues) is a well-established phenomenon. 
  However, the underlying principles underlying this behavior remain unclear. 
  This study investigates the underlying structure that drives the lambda-value decay. 
  We show the decrease in lambda values is driven by the cross-coupling terms 
  between different output channels rather than the individual input channels. 
  In particular, we find that the spectral density of these matrices can be represented 
  by a specific type of matrix whose eigenvector eigenvalue decomposition reveals 
  the rank of the original matrices, providing a direct connection to tensor decomposition. 
  As a result, we are able to analyze the eigenvalue decay and demonstrate its 
  asymptotic behavior as it approaches an exponential distribution. 
  Additionally, we develop a novel algorithm based on this understanding, 
  which leverages the natural ordering of lambda values to focus on the most 
  significant components, resulting in a dramatic improvement in performance. 
  Compared to existing methods, this algorithm exhibits superior performance in 
  component identification, with an order of magnitude improvement in the number 
  required to achieve a given level of accuracy. 
  This advantage becomes increasingly pronounced with growing tensor size. 
  In particular, a 16x increase in accuracy is achievable with only a 2x increase 
  in the number of model training iterations. 
  This algorithm has tangible benefits in reducing memory usage by 2 orders of magnitude 
  while maintaining the same level of accuracy in real-world applications. 
  As such, it has already been successfully integrated into several critical systems. 
  We are now making this algorithm widely available.

We have also observed that the change in a particular measure of the size of the lattice's entropy over time can give us an approximate estimate of the time it takes for the system to relax to a non-equilibrium steady state. In this study, we investigate the size of Boolean formulas required to replicate specific functions, focusing on functions whose own complexity is polynomial in relation to input variables.  To this end, we develop a method for determining the circuit complexity of functions with an exponential input size, even though similar calculations are generally challenging due to the intricacies of circuit complexity analysis.  Our approach is inspired by recent advances in approximating the rank of specific matrix types, including Gaussian matrices and Toeplitz matrices, which have wide applications in combinatorial structures, number theory, and algebraic geometry.  We demonstrate that the circuit complexity of certain classes of functions, including those defined by recursive relations, modular operations, and discrete logarithms, can be appreciably quantified.  In particular, we find that a specific sequence involving recursive relations, known as the Fibonacci sequence, has a circuit complexity that grows at a polynomial rate, in contrast to expectations of an exponential growth pattern.  Our analysis also extends to functions generated by Gaussian matrices and their modifications, for which we establish approximations that further provide insights into the structure of these matrices.  In addition, we explore connections between the circuit complexity of functions and the computational resources required to solve related problems in number theory, such as solving modular multilinear equations and computing discrete logs in their entirety, rather than specific log values.  Overall, our studies highlight the diverse applications of advanced analytical techniques in combinatorial structures, providing a framework for more extensive research into the intricacies of circuit complexity in physics and computer science.  We also develop a method for estimating the circuit complexity of functions with an exponential input size, which can be thought of as placing the Boshernitzan-Sarzio sequence within a broader class of structured sequences with polynomial complexity. a fundamental parameter in the standard model, whose precise measurement in lepton scattering processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is being examined. To achieve a highly accurate measurement, it's essential to control systematic uncertainties in the reconstruction of transverse momentum. Amongst the dominant uncertainties in this measurement, we identify those associated with the proton structure function and demonstrate the feasibility of reducing them through the use of Roma, a weighted functional approach that utilizes weighted Lagrange multipliers. By employing Roma in conjunction with synthetic data, we illustrate the potential for a 0.5\% precision on the weak mixing angle in lepton scattering processes at the LHC. To attain a precision of the order 0.1\%, we propose generating precise functional parameters via global QCD fits to deep inelastic scattering data and predict that in such a case, Roma could yield a 0.1\% precision on the weak mixing angle, solely from the control regions, without even analyzing actual LHC data. To achieve this level of precision, however, it will be necessary to minimize other systematic uncertainties to a degree of 0.05\% or better. To this end, we are also exploring methods of reducing further the uncertainty associated with the Roma approach, such as utilizing quark correlation functions and reweighting techniques. In the process, we are simultaneously investigating how to combine the Roma approach with other systematic uncertainty reduction techniques employed in current LHC analyses. This paper explores another manifestation of the Riemann Hypothesis, referred to as the Sato-Tate Conjecture for abelian varieties, which involves the distribution of points on these varieties within finite fields. Both the Riemann Hypothesis and the Sato-Tate Conjecture imply that the distribution of these points follows a specific probability measure, which we will call the natural measure. Our main contribution is to demonstrate that there are infinitely many zeros of a specific type for a family of elliptic curves defined over the rational numbers if the natural measure of these curves does not lead to a uniform distribution over the unit circle in the complex plane. This result provides an alternative to the recent findings of other mathematicians, which showed that the zero densities implied by the Riemann Hypothesis or the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture lead to measures that do not result in a uniform distribution over the unit circle. We also discuss the connection between our result and the recent findings, as well as the potential growth of the zeros in the complex plane that it suggests. Additionally, we explore the implications of our result for the family of Mordell-Shaferevich curves, which includes curves defined by specific polynomial equations with large degree, and demonstrate that the majority of these curves have a high number of points in the complex plane, making them extremely rigid. We also consider the variation of these curves in the complex plane and show that it is driven by the growth of zeros in the complex plane. This, in turn, leads to the conclusion that the majority of hyperelliptic curves of high genus also have a large number of points in the complex plane, which suggests that they are highly rigid and have a limited variation in the complex plane. This result can be seen as a manifestation of the idea that the arithmetic of these curves is governed by the natural measure, which, as mentioned earlier, is associated with the Riemann Hypothesis and the Sato-Tate Conjecture. This, in turn, implies that the majority of these curves have a massive number of points in the finite field F_q, which could have significant implications for the study of their automorphism groups and Hecke operators. This, in turn, could also lead to a deeper understanding of the fundamental theorem of Galois cohomology proposed by Serre,

ogeneous Quantum Annealing Correction code, 
  a recent pseudodimensional Quantum Annealing simulator designed to mitigate 
  thermal effects, now for a three-spin Heisenberg model in one dimension. 
  We assess its performance in comparison to a state-of-the-art art BDQAO approach 
  by evaluating the accuracy of both methods in simulating a full Quantum Annealing 
  process for various Heisenberg models with different numbers of spins. 
  Specifically, we examine systems comprising anywhere from three to sixty-three 
  spins, investigating the efficacy of each code along the way. 
  We conclude by exploring the potential applications of the Erezos code. 
  The Erezos code is available at https://github.com/qudev20/Erezos. 
  In particular, we found that both BDQAO and Erezos codes yield nearly identical 
  results when evaluating the energy of Heisenberg models following a full Quantum 
  Annealing process. In fact, the average energy values obtained from both codes 
  differ by no more than 10^{-4} from the actual values across all simulated 
  models. Furthermore, we found that both codes demonstrate the same quadratic 
  growth in simulation execution time as the number of spins squared. 
  The Erezos code is implemented using the Quantum Circuit Library qCircuit, 
  a Python-based open-source package for defining and visualizing Quantum 
  Circuits, now also available with an additional method for generating 
  intermediate results during simulation execution. 
  We also introduce a new approach, which we call the "Fourier-based" method, 
  for correcting the effects of Qubit Interference during simulation execution. 
  We derive this method from the original parent algorithm, which involves 
  a multi-Qubit Interference Correction step that uses a library of all possible 
  intermediate results for a particular Heisenberg model. 
  However, this approach is computationally expensive as it involves looking 
  up multiple entries in a large database during simulation execution. 
  In contrast, the Fourier-based method is much more efficient as it involves 
  a single database lookup for each spin once per simulation execution. 
  We also provide a detailed analysis of the Fourier-based method, which we 
  derive from the original parent algorithm. 
  The Erezos code is designed to be highly customizable and comes with a 
  built-in option for using either the original parent algorithm or the 
  Fourier-based method for Qubit Interference Correction.

of black phosphorus is highly dependent on orientation and contains complex anisotropic effects. To fully understand these effects, we've conducted a comprehensive study using first-principents density functional theory. Our findings show that black phosphorus exhibits substantial anisotropic second-order nonlinear optical properties, along with a lack of any third-order nonlinearity. The distribution of optical second-harmonic generation in black phosphorus reveals significant $\chi^{(2)}_{xyz}$ component, combined with the rare occurrence of $\chi^{(2)}_{xxxy}$ and $\chi^{(2)}_{zzzz}$ components. The microscopic origins of these effects are attributed to the unique orientation of phosphorus atoms and the resulting hybridization of $p$ and $s$ orbital interactions. This research provides a clear understanding of the underlying physics and points out potential applications in controlling the nonlinear optical properties by means of external pressure and layer stacking methods. Overall, black phosphorus is identified as a material with promising nonlinear optical properties, along with its potential for integrating stacked layered structures to enhance $\chi^{(2)}$ capability by means of van der Waals bonding. This research also highlights the limitations of density functional theory and the need for accounting many-body effects through the use of GW method or functional renormalization group. This study is conducted using the plane-wave basis approach within the local density approximation and checked for reliability using a supercell approach within the generalized gradient approximation. Our findings are further validated by means of experimental second-harmonic generation and Raman scattering results. This research paves the way for exploring and controlling the nonlinear optical properties of black phosphorus. This work is done by the first-author team and the corresponding authors are Q. This analysis is set within the context of an obstacle problem, where the admissible set is defined by a variational inequality. We have established that solutions to this problem possess higher regularity properties than those previously established by Di PlAccommand. In particular, we have demonstrated that the time derivative of the solution belongs to $L^2(0,T;L^{\infty}(\Omega))$. Secondly, we have shown that a specific condition on the coefficient $\gamma$ is necessary for the problem in question. This condition, which was not previously known, is associated with the regularity of the solutions and ensures that the time derivative of the solution does not exhibit jump behavior over time. This research was inspired by a previous study by Bénilan, Blida, and Souleti, who established a lower bound for the space in which the time derivative of the solution belongs when the coefficient $\gamma$ has limited variation, but they did not provide a sharp estimate. In contrast, we have derived a precise estimate when the coefficient $\gamma$ exhibits infinite variation, as is the case with the S.K. Scott model. We have achieved this result by introducing a new method that is based on characterizing the solutions using the viscosity sense. This characterization allows us to obtain the maximum possible value for the space to which the time derivative of the solution belongs when the coefficient $\gamma$ exhibits a given type of discontinuity. This method is general and can be applied to a broad class of problems with degenerate parabolic equations in the sense of viscosity. This research has also been motivated by a desire to extend the previous results to a wider context, as it provides the estimates on the regularity of the solutions that are necessary to establish the existence and properties of the solutions to a variety of problems with inequalities and constraints, including problems with state constraints, a variant of the minimal surface problem, and a variant of the Euler equation. Our analysis reveals that the distribution of advantages from PPP projects varies depending on the project in question. While some projects primarily benefit private companies, others mainly gain from partnerships with public entities. The literature also indicates that the emergence of PPPs is often attributed to the limitations of traditional infrastructure financing methods. In response, we propose an empirical model to predict the outcomes of PPP projects for different stakeholders. Our data covers 789 projects from the World Bank's PPP pipeline and shows that while private companies tend to take on more risks in PPP projects, they also reap greater rewards. In contrast, public entities appear to prioritize projects with shorter construction periods and those that generate more revenue. Our findings suggest that the benefits of PPP projects are largely determined by the characteristics of the project itself, rather than its financing structure. Consequently, it's crucial to assess projects based on their inherent merits before considering PPP financing.  The literature suggests that the distribution of PPP benefits favors private companies that assume significant risks in projects with high potential returns. In such cases, the tax benefits associated with PPPs can be particularly lucrative. In contrast, public entities tend to prioritize projects with established revenue streams and shorter construction periods. The diversity of PPP projects makes it essential to evaluate each on its individual merits rather than relying on the reputation of private companies. The question of whether private companies that benefit from PPPs are truly taking on sufficient risk remains a subject of debate. The literature indicates that the tax advantages of PPPs can be significant but neglects to account for the potential hidden costs incurred by public entities. The study's data reveals that while private companies tend to prioritize projects with higher potential returns, they also favor projects with longer construction periods that minimize their upfront costs. In response to these concerns, it's possible to modify the proposed empirical model to predict the outcomes of PPP projects for different stakeholders. However, the underlying issue of model overfitting hindering generalizability on real-world data remains a significant challenge. To tackle this problem, researchers typically adopt three separate strategies: regulating models through statistical methods, utilizing real-world data for training, and employing psycholinguistic knowledge in question and answer contexts. Yet, these approaches have distinct limitations and don't guarantee robust, efficient performance in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we propose a novel approach, EXQAS, which leverages the underlying reasoning process in question answering by incorporating a module that identifies and selects relevant information from context through description generation. This module is powered by a simple, locally-trained model that employs a minimal set of psycholinguistic features to assess the coherence of generated descriptions with actual answers. As a result, EXQAS achieves superior performance compared to multiple baselines across three different datasets, showcasing the advantages of our approach in tackling model overfitting in practical applications.  We also conduct an in-depth analysis of non-performing instances to gain valuable insights into the underlying reasoning process and potential weaknesses of our approach. Notably, EXQAS's performance is found to significantly improve when trained on smaller datasets, demonstrating its robustness in preventing model overfitting. To further cement the theoretical foundations of our approach, we develop a new method for evaluating the coherence of generated descriptions using BERT, which we believe can be applied to related tasks in Natural Language Inference. We have made EXQAS's code and models publicly available on GitHub at the specified URL.  We believe that our novel EXQAS approach has vast potential for enhancing the efficacy of large-scale NLP models in real-world, real-time applications. electron system in
Ga$_{1-x}$In$_x$As/GaAs doped heterostructures were examined using
Conductivity Tensor Spectroscopy. A significant anisotropy in the magnetic
field's effect on carrier transport was discovered, which is essential for
understanding and controlling spin-triplet phenomena in these structures.
By conducting measurements at cryogenic temperatures with varying
magnetic field orientations, our experiment accurately determined the
electron system's spatial extent and local magnetic field strength, which
are crucial parameters influencing the system's magnetic properties.
Our findings indicate that despite the electron system's two-dimensional
nature, it exhibits unique one-dimensional behavior in the presence of a
strong magnetic field aligned with the doped heterstructure's interface.
This unique phenomenon arises from the precise control of doping and
interface quality, which together eliminate carrier scattering and allow
for the examination of highly anisotropic magnetoresistance. Our study
has significant implications for understanding and manipulating the quasi-
two-dimensional electron system's magnetic properties in Ga$_{1-x}$In$_x$
As/GaAs doped heterostructures. This understanding is critical for
controlling spin-triplet phenomena, supervision of quantum phase shifts,
and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle-induced two-dimensional magnetoresistance. Our experimental results are accompanied by comprehensive numerical simulations of conductivity tensor spectroscopy in the presence of a magnetic field. This simulation tool can be applied to experimentally study various scattering mechanisms, the effect of interface roughness on carrier behavior, and carrier distribution in these structures. Our study provides a solid foundation for further theoretical and experimental investigation of spin-triplet phenomena, Heisenberg's uncertainty principle-induced two-dimensional magnetoresistance, and quantum phase shifts in these systems. This knowledge is indispensable for developing precise, large-scale devices that control spin-triplet phenomena and quantum phase shifts. Experimental details, including measurement techniques and material growth, are presented in the Appendices.   a highly sensitive technique called continuous-time Ramsey sequencing, 
  and a less sensitive technique called pulsed EPR contrast enhancement.

Conventional approaches often employ simplifications, such as streamfunction or vorticity formulations, which assume incompressible and constant-density fluids. In contrast, our algorithm uses a novel combination of discrete operators applied to conservative forms of the Navier-Stokes equations, allowing us to directly simulate the behavior of fluids with changing density, as seen in the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability. By leveraging this method, we have performed comprehensive simulations of the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, encompassing a broad range of flow velocities, free surface heights, and viscosity levels. Our findings align with previous study results when those assumptions are met, and our simulations reveal distinct, nonlinear, and rotating 'eye' structures in the head region, in addition to the previously noted rotor and Kelvin-Helmholtz billows. We have also observed the formation of a high-velocity, thin-layer rotor in the free surface and a rotating, thin-layer 'eye' in both incompressible and compressible simulations. Furthermore, our results include detailed quantitative data on rotor size, eye size, and Kelvin-Helmholtz billow spacing in relation to free surface height, viscosity, and flow velocity ratios. These outcomes can be analyzed using our non-linear, two-dimensional rotor model, which is subsequently extended to a model incorporating the free surface and viscosity. This free surface and rotor model is itself part of a broader, self-consistent, two-dimensional model of the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability. We have validated our models against our direct numerical simulation data and have also performed a second-order analysis of the rotor model to explain the observed patterns of mass stripping and rotor growth in the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability. The outcomes of our models are in line with previous findings based on simplified, analytical approaches, yet our direct simulation method provides a more comprehensive understanding of the non-linear, three-dimensional rotor dynamics in the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability. We believe that our method can be utilised to simulate other free surface, fluid dynamics problems characterized by rotor structures, such as those seen in and in relation to jet or shear layer instabilities in both incompressible and compressible flows. The knowledge gained from the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability in the head region, specifically with regard to rotor, eye, and Kelvin-Helmholtz billow structures, can be immediately applied to improve existing models of wind turbine or helicopter rotor tip vortex dynamics and to shed light on mass stripping

We successfully bypass this difficulty by choosing a specific non-minimal coupling where the number of degrees of freedom is conserved during inflation, leading to a direct relationship between the Bardeen parameter and the perturbation in the scalar field. As a result, we can determine the scalar perturbation straightforwardly without needing to solve the perturbed Einstein equations. The conservation of degrees of freedom during inflation also eliminates the perturbation in the metric during the inflationary phase. The subsequent stage, the oscillatory phase, is modeled using two possible scenarios: a sudden end of inflation where the number of degrees of freedom returns to normal in an instantaneous transition, and a gradual transition where the increase in the Bardeen parameter occurs in sync with the growing number of degrees of freedom during the oscillatory phase. We find that the former case yields a value of the tensor-to-tilt ratio (tns) in excess of 0.037, which can be obtained when the oscillation lasts for roughly 3-4 cycles. In contrast, the latter case gives rise to slower growth of tns, with values exceeding 0.01 for a longer duration of 5-6 cycles. The associated spectral indices of the scalar perturbation (ns) remain less than 0.98 in both cases. We also determine the optimal amplitude of the Bardeen parameter (A_Φ) in both scenarios, with possible values ranging from 5.05E-5 to 4.86E-4, which can be compared with recent findings based on the Planck dataset. The two cases can be distinguished based on their corresponding values of the quadratic index (ns-1), with the former case yielding values less than -0.01 and the latter case yielding values exceeding -0.01. The associated mass scales during the oscillatory phase fall within the GUT or TeV scales, with the former applicable to the sudden exit case and the latter applicable to the gradual exit case. The two scenarios can be further analyzed based on their power spectra of the Bardeen parameter, with the sudden exit case exhibiting a power spectrum dominated by the adiabatic contribution during the oscillatory phase and the gradual exit case exhibiting a power spectrum dominated by the radiation dominance during the oscillatory phase. gamma-ray binary systems containing compact objects have become extremely fascinating subjects. These systems generally fall into three categories: containing black holes or neutron stars in binary orbits with either massive companions or low-mass companions. While the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope has detected gamma-ray emissions from over a hundred sources, its sensitivity to weak signals limits its ability to detect systems with high orbital periods or small binary separations. At frequencies below 1 GHz, highly sensitive radio telescopes such as the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder or the Future Wideband Arecibo Spectrographic and Array System will be capable of detecting emissions from systems with large orbital periods. However, processing vast amounts of data from these telescopes in real-time is an significant challenge. Due to the lengthy acquisition time of these images, considering rolling shutter effects is now also crucial.  These distortions can be accounted for by introducing an additional variable in reconstruction algorithms or using specialized sequences, although such approaches either limit flexibility or employ complicated optimization solvers.  We present a novel method that leverages machine learning to provide accurate estimates of rolling shutter distortions, thereby unlocking flexible and efficient phase sorting reconstructions.  By training a network on training data featuring diverse acquisition timings and field strengths, we achieved promising results in our experiments, with rolling shutter correction performed at minimal additional computational expense.  Our approach also generalizes well to new datasets, as evidenced by successful applications to datasets acquired with different sequences and at different field strengths.  We have made our code publicly available on GitHub, in the hope that it may serve as a foundation for developing MRI hardware-efficient, robust, and precise phase sorting reconstructions.  We have also included quantitative evaluation metrics obtained with human readers, to demonstrate that our method yields comparable image quality to references obtained through reference-free reconstruction, as validated by both automatic and human evaluations.  Our results suggest that employing a machine learning-based rolling shutter correction yields comparable performance to more complex solutions, highlighting the potential of this approach for real-world implementations.  We have also presented preliminary evidence that our method can be applied to other MRI processing tasks, such as B0 map estimation, by incorporating additional inputs, as we have shown that combining B0 maps with cine MRI allows for their quantitative analysis, as validated by human evaluations. \section{Introduction}

The Standard Model (SM) is the current, most comprehensive theoretical
description of particle physics phenomena. However, the absence of certain
physical phenomena suggests the existence of beyond-SM physics. In this work,
we focus on supersymmetric (SUSY) partners of top and bottom quarks. These
partners are among the lightest SUSY particles and have the largest
production cross-sections. Their detection is feasible at the Large Hadron
Collider (LHC) with a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV.

The search for top and bottom partners is conducted in final states featuring
one charged lepton (either an electron or a muon) and numerous jets. To
account for the SM background, advanced methods are employed, primarily
based on machine learning techniques. The analysis is performed on an
integrated luminosity of 139 fb^-1, collected during proton-proton collisions
at the LHC, operated by CERN.

Our analysis focuses on satellite galaxies weighing less than 10^8 times the mass of our sun. We find that the mass function of these satellites aligns with power law distributions observed in real galaxies, despite aurora's slightly different distribution. Our results suggest a distinct category of low-mass satellites that were formed through the cooling of gas in the early stages of the universe, rather than through the gravitational fragmentation of more massive galaxies. We estimate this cool-core scenario accounts for approximately 20% of satellites in the mass range 10^6-10^8 solar masses. Notably, aurora does not reproduce the observed peak in the mass function at solar mass scales. We also observe a apparent peak in the mass spectrum at ~5% of the mass of the Sgr dwarf, which may be related to the way aurora represents the disruption of satellites by the gravitational influence of the galaxy. Our analysis of satellite galactic evolution reveals that the majority of galaxies in the mass range 10^8-10^11 solar masses exhibit a similar evolutionary trajectory, characterized by an initial passive period followed by an active period marked by the absorption of a satellite of a certain mass, and finally, a period of gas absorption and eventual star formation shutdown. We interpret this progression as the result of a single massive satellite being broken down into smaller pieces over time. We believe that future observations of satellite galaxies will benefit from a distinction between the cool-core and disrupted categories. We estimate that the most significant satellites in the mass range 10^8-10^11 solar masses account for a minimum of 20% of a galaxy's mass, and a maximum of 50% considering the influence of gas absorption. We also find that the most substantial satellites typically have masses in the range 10^9-10^10.5 solar masses, and as such, a peak in the mass function at this scale may be difficult to detect. We propose that the relationship between the mass of a galaxy and its most significant satellite can be described by a power law with an index of ~1.5, and predict that future observations will reveal the peak in the mass function at solar mass scales as an illusion resulting from the fragmentation of more massive galaxies. We also highlight the importance of distinguishing between satellites that were formed through the cooling of gas and those that were formed as a result of the disruption of more massive galaxies

Conversely, when prices are relatively prime, the no--arbitrage property holds in a market that allows for short selling but not the sale of negative quantities. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that in a market with no--arbitrage opportunities, the prices of all possible states that can arise in the future are determinable from the current prices, and this fact has important implications for the pricing of contingent claims. In this context, the study also investigates the concept of a market's memory and its connection to prices that are relatively prime, as well as the condition under which prices that are relatively prime guarantee the existence of a strategy

  We introduce the concept of model resistance, measuring a model's ability to perform well
  even when inputs are slightly altered.
  Building on this idea, we create the Model Resistance Test Bed (MRTB) to evaluate
  model performance under various types of noise across three image classification tasks.
  Our findings show that even slight distortions can significantly impact model performance.
  We also discover that wide deep networks exhibit higher model resistance than narrow deep
  networks and that training models with high resistance leads to better real-world results. 
  MRTB's transparent design allows us to incorporate model resistance into existing metrics
  or utilize it as a standalone performance indicator. 
  We make MRTB publicly available at \url{http://mrdb.csail.mit.edu}. 
  The code for training and evaluating models with/without MR in mind is available at \url{https://github.com/vysudana/Model-Resistance}.

  resistance in vision.

assembly problem asks for the minimum number of dominoes required to tile an n x n grid, where each domino can be oriented either horizontally or vertically. It has been proven that this domino tiling requirement is equivalent to the number of ways to walk along a grid from the upper left corner to the lower right corner, where each step is either down by one unit or right by one unit, without backtracking. This problem can also be reinterpreted in terms of binary trees, where each internal node represents a turn in the walk and its children correspond to the possible directions of the next step. The number of such binary trees can be expressed in terms of the Catalan number C_(n-1). Another related problem in the planar assembly context involves arranging n pairs of nested parentheses, which can be translated into a binary tree where each internal node has two children and the root corresponds to the starting point. The number of these binary trees can be represented as the nth Catalan number C_n. The more recent paradigm of population-based learning aims to find a single model that effectively accommodates diverse data points by focusing on the common ground among them. In this paper, a new method is introduced that combines the benefits of both approaches, allowing for the analysis of individual results while maintaining a single model trained on population-level characteristics. key challenge in genomics.  Beyond identifying individual genes, researchers are working to map elements that influence non-coding regions, which account for the majority of the genome.  To address this, researchers have employed genome editing to create a comprehensive, high-resolution map of non-coding DNA functionality across the mouse genome.  By comparing mice with specific genetic modifications to their wild-type counterparts, researchers can determine the effects of individual DNA elements on various physiological traits.  Using this approach, they have mapped the functional elements underlying the development and function of different cell types, as well as tissue-specific gene expression.  Interestingly, many of these non-coding elements lie near genes that they do not directly influence, suggesting they play a role in controlling distant, unrelated genes through secondary effects on the transcriptome.  To better understand these complex genetic interactions, researchers have developed an approach that integrates data from genome editing, RNA sequencing, and proteomics.  By analyzing the effects of DNA modifications on the levels of proteins produced across the mouse body, they have identified the functional elements responsible for the production of specific proteins and have mapped their underlying non-coding DNA.  This has revealed that many protein-coding genes are influenced by elements located in non-coding regions, with some being as far as 1 million base pairs away.  To visualize and explore these complex genetic interactions, researchers have created an online tool called ATETRACK, which allows users to examine the non-coding elements affecting specific proteins or groups of proteins.  This approach has also been applied to humans and other organisms, providing a framework for understanding the functional organization of genetic information at a global scale.  By studying the non-coding elements responsible for the production of specific proteins, researchers have identified many that are associated with particular physiological traits or cell types.  To further explore this, they have developed a machine learning model that predicts the non-coding elements influencing particular proteins based on their genetic characteristics.  This has revealed that many non-coding elements are organized into families with shared characteristics that determine their functionality, with some families being specific to particular organisms.  To examine the evolutionary history of these non-coding elements, researchers have analyzed the sequences of ancient DNA from extinct species and have found that some of the non-coding elements influencing current protein production also affected protein production in these ancient species.  This suggests that many non-coding elements have remained largely unchanged for millions of years and have played a key role in the development and function of different cell types and tissue-specific gene expression. A general scalar field theory drives this perturbation, and we compute the related power spectrum for both the adiabatic and entropic components through the use of multiple gauge invariant variables. A gauged shift symmetry in the scalar potential leads to the formation of initial black holes during the phase transition, and we examine the power spectra before and during this transition. As a result, this signature can serve as an exceptional tool for investigating the history of the Universe, particularly during the period between the Big Bang and the present day. However, accurately calculating the 21-cm signal relies on intricate astrophysical processes and their associated uncertainties, making it crucial to develop detailed models of the interstellar medium. These models can be tested against observational data from the current and future generations of radio telescopes, which are designed to detect this signal. In this paper, we present a comprehensive code, called ``calm'', that simulates the 21-cm signal based on a two-zone model of the interstellar medium, incorporating gas phases with molecular and atomic hydrogen. We apply this code to a large dataset of approximately 10,000 simulated quasistar formations, and make the calm code publicly available online at https://github.com/changhaseo/calm.  The findings from our code can be readily utilized with existing 21-cm signal simulations, and we also provide a simple algorithm to generate mock observations from these simulations, which can be employed with upcoming large-scale 21-cm experiments. Our results demonstrate that future detections will primarily focus on the spin temperature, and we predict that R.T.S. (signal-to-noise ratio) values of ten or greater can be achieved in experiments spanning a week to a month in duration. Furthermore, we find that achieving a detection with an accuracy of one degree Kelvin on the kinetic temperature will likely surpass the technical limitations of telescopes in the near future, and we propose a design for a next-generation radio telescope capable of achieving this goal.  The calm code can be utilized to generate mock observations for a wide range of quasistar formations based on their spectral properties, and we make these simulations publicly available online at https://www.shao.ac.cn/~changhaseo/data.html.  We also suggest that combining calm with existing 21-cm signal simulations, and employing a semi-parametric model to analyze these simulations in conjunction with future observations, will yield quasistar formation histograms with accuracy levels of 70% or greater.  Finally, we propose that developing techniques for recovering the physical and chemical conditions of the interstellar medium from future 21-cm experiments will yield substantial scientific returns from these experiments. These predictions are frequently made using machine learning models trained on operational system data.  However, the data required for training is often restricted due to security constraints within the application's domain, leading to the lack of effective performance prediction tools for many Web applications.  Researchers have addressed this challenge by gaining access to a system administrator's account, extracting performance data from the application server, and utilizing this data to train a model that predicts performance problems.  Our research confirmed that it's possible to accurately predict performance issues even when access to user data is limited.  We found that the lack of user data does present some challenges, but these can be overcome by utilizing techniques such as stacking generalizers.  Furthermore, we discovered that performance-related information already present in the application server's logs can significantly enhance predictive accuracy.  Our results indicate that using log data in conjunction with server metrics yields a 23% improvement in predictive model accuracy compared to using server metrics alone.  The discovery of session-related variables that influence application performance was also significant, though these variables are rarely considered in related work.  Our research further revealed that certain application performance issues are difficult to anticipate based on system data, due to their sudden onset.  We established that many of these issues are likely the result of external events, such as DDoS attacks, and suggest that a system-level approach is necessary to effectively predict performance issues.  The findings of our research have implications for designing more scalable and secure Web applications, and highlight the financial benefits of preventing performance-related problems. Our solution involves a two-phase approach for an approximate solution and a third phase for refinement. In the first phase, we establish a lower bound on the minimum weighted connected coverage cost and use a randomized algorithm to obtain an approximate solution within a factor of two of this lower bound with a high degree of probability. Recent research has identified that, in many cases, single-modal data itself is sufficient to achieve comparable performance to that of multimodal data.  However, we discovered that, even when single-modal and multimodal data have similar performance on various benchmarks, the multimodal data consistently learns more effective classifiers that generalize better when compared to their single-modal counterparts.
